  STAFF COMMENTS:

  City Manager de Geus stated our landscaping equipment contractor, American Heritage,
  has been utilizing zero emission equipment this past month around City Hall and the
  Library and it is working well. American Green Zone Alliance will be assisting staff with
  developing a citywide landscaping Request for Proposal and they have been shadowing
  the City's current landscape maintenance providers, Brightview and American Heritage,
  to ensure the scope of services accurately describes the city needs and will include the
  expectation that we move towards zero emission landscaping equipment.

  Related to COVID-19, Mr. de Geus noted that the positivity rate and cases have been
  decreasing. In addition, the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health released a
  revised Public Health Order that removes the indoor masking mandate for vaccinated
  individuals on Friday, February 25, 2022 with verification of vaccination status. This will
  assist staff with bringing City Council back into Council Chambers for in-person meetings
  in March.

  For Pedestrian Safety, Mr. de Geus mentioned that outreach and education continues
  with some targeted outreach to the Three Springs Neighborhood on utilizing the
  Pedestrian Hybrid Beacon. Targeted speed enforcement continues daily with some night-
  time enforcement, which has resulted in issuance of citations. He further noted that
  preliminary designs for sidewalks on Lindero Canyon Road between Agoura Road and
  Baronsgate Road and between Whim Drive to Hedgewall Drive is underway. Also, a small
  segment of sidewalk on the corner of Lindero Canyon Road and Agoura Road to the bus
  stop by the Chevron Station will soon be underway.

MONTHLY DEPARTMENTAL REPORTS:

1.  Sheriff's Department Report

  Deputy Brian Knott presented the Sheriff Department's crime and traffic report for
  January 2022. Lieutenant Chad Watters reported that the Lakeside Wine and
  Spirits burglary case has resulted in eight suspects arrested. The suspects were
  involved in burglaries at 35 other businesses in Ventura and Los Angeles Counties.
  Nighttime speeding measures continue to be addressed with multiple speeding
  tickets issued. He reminded residents to always lock their vehicles and not leave
  a purse in an unlocked car.

2.  Fire Department Report

  Assistant Fire Chief Drew Smith presented the Fire Department's report for
  January 2022. Community Services Liaison Megan Currier reported on Public
  Education stating that the Explorer program application process will begin in March
  and a Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) class will be scheduled for
  April/May.

3.  Chamber of Commerce Report

  Director of Government Affairs and Tourism Adam Haverstock and highlighted the
  following Greater Conejo Valley Chamber of Commerce activities and events.
  Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) equipment (masks and hand sanitizer) are
  for available for businesses. The order form is on the Chamber website and all
  local businesses are eligible. Assembly Bill 1234 passed in 2016 mandates that
  businesses with five or more employees offer a retirement plan. A webinar on this
  topic will be held on February 24, 2022 at noon. The Chamber is currently
  accepting applications for their annual Awards Gala and the nomination link is on
  their website. On April 8, 2022 the Chamber will host its annual Regional Economic
  Forecast, tickets for sale on their website.

4.  Library Report

  Manager of the Westlake Village Daniel K. Ludwig Library Julie Frieze presented
  the Library report for January 2022. She reported that Library Hours of Operation
  will adjust on March 14, 2022 to be Tuesday and Wednesdays 12-8 pm, Thursday
  - Saturdays 10 am - 6 pm and closed on Sunday and Mondays.

  PUBLIC HEARINGS:

  1.  CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT NO. 96-003, Modification 3; RESOLUTION NO.
  2237-22

  City Manager de Geus introduced the item and Associate Planner Sinkula
  presented the request for approving Modification No. 3 of Conditional Use Permit
  No. 96-003, authorizing the continued operation of an existing wireless
  telecommunications facility, the replacement of three existing antennas with three
  new antennas, and the installation of three new remote radio units and two new
  equipment cabinets on an existing rooftop wireless telecommunications site
  located at 5716 Corsa Avenue.

  Associate Planner Sinkula reported the facility operated by T-Mobile consists of
  six antennas grouped into three sectors that are mounted to the rooftop and
  screened by a parapet style roof. The current CUP is set to expire on September
  27, 2022, and the applicant has requested an extension of the permit term as part
  of the request to modify the equipment on the site. The site also includes antennas
  for two other telecommunication companies and those requests are not part of this
  hearing.

  On December 2, 2020, the Land Use Committee comprised of Councilmember
  Halpern and then Mayor Pro Tern Mcsweeney requested that the applicant provide
  additional screening for the equipment to improve aria! views from the Community
  Park. On January 3, 2022, the applicant submitted revised plans that proposed to
  screen the antennas within three new radome structures consistent with the
  screening provided for the other existing wireless telecommunications facilities on
  the rooftop. Staff reviewed the revised submittal and determined that the proposed
  new radome structures were much wider than the existing radome structures on
  the roof and significantly more noticeable from views from Russell Ranch Road
  than the facility is presently without the radome structures.

  The applicant has requested a ten-year permit term, which is consistent with
  requirements of State planning law (Government Code§ 65964(b)) that proscribe
  unreasonable limitations on permit durations for wireless telecommunications
  facilities and specify that permit terms of less than ten years are presumed to be
  unreasonable. She reported that staff was unaware of any complaints associated
  with the subject facility and recommended approval of the CUP request to extend
  the permit term and modify the equipment onsite as described above, and further
  recommend a permit term of ten years.

  Councilmember Honig moved to adopt Resolution No. 2237-22 "A Resolution of
  the City Council of the City of Westlake Village approving Modification No. 3 of
  Conditional Use Permit No. 96-003, authorizing the continued operation of an
  existing wireless telecommunications facility, the replacement of three existing

2.  ADOPTION OF NORTH BUSINESS PARK SPECIFIC PLAN COST RECOVERY
  FEES: RESOLUTION NO. 2238-22

  City Manager de Geus introduced the item and Planning Director Forbes
  presented the request for establishing fees to recover the cost to the City for
  preparing, adopting, administering, and maintaining the North Business Park
  Specific Plan (NBPSP).

  Planning Director Forbes reported in June 2020, the City Council adopted the
  NBPSP to establish a vision and development framework to guide reinvestment in
  the specific plan area. Working with Stanley R. Hoffman Associates, cost recovery
  fees were established and were discussed in October 2021 with City Council.

  California Government Code Section 65456(a) authorizes cities to establish and
  collect fees for costs associated with preparing, adopting, administering, and
  maintaining a specific plan. Stanley R. Hoffman Associates determined that the
  City incurred a cost of $1,308,858 over 10 years to prepare and adopt the NBPSP
  and its EIR, including consultant costs, staff time, and overhead (in 2021 dollars).
  The estimated cost to administer and maintain the NBPSP over the next 20 years
  is about $220,776 (in 2021 dollars). This results in a total cost of $1,529,634 to be
  recovered, adjusted to 2021 dollars. He also mentioned that the City was awarded
  a $160,000 Senate Bill (SB) 2 Planning Grant to partially offset the cost of
  preparing the NBPSP, reducing the amount to be recovered to $1,369,634. He
  recommended the City Council adopt fees intended to achieve full cost recovery
  which are $1,480.03 per residential unit, $1,007.35/1,000 square feet of non-
  residential floor area, with a 2% annual escalator to account for inflation.

NEW BUSINESS:

1.  NOTIFICATION OF INTENT TO COMPLY WITH SHORT-LIVED CLIMATE
  POLLUTANTS REGULATIONS; RESOLUTION NO. 2239-22

  City Manager de Geus introduced the item and Planning Director Forbes
  requested Council approval of a Notification of Intent to Comply (NOIC) with the
  State's Short-Lived Climate Pollutants (SLCP) Regulations pursuant to Senate Bill
  (SB) 1383 and SB 619 and directing staff to submit the NOIC by the deadline of
  March 1, 2022.

  Planning Director Forbes reported that SB 1383 was signed into law in 2016 and
  established methane reduction targets as part of a Statewide effort to reduce
  greenhouse gas emissions from short-lived climate pollutants such as organic
  waste. SB 1383 requires a 50 percent reduction from 2014 levels in the amount of
  organic waste sent to landfills by 2020 and a 75 percent reduction by 2025. Further,
  SB 1383 requires 20 percent of edible food, which would otherwise be disposed
  of, be recovered for human consumption by 2025.

  Starting in 2022, cities are required to implement and oversee programs to ensure
  that certain food service businesses donate edible food to food recovery
  organizations. Cities will be required to have an enforcement mechanism to ensure
  compliance with the SLCP Regulations, and the State will levy penalties and fines
  of up to $10,000 per day on jurisdictions that fail to comply.

  SB 619 provides an opportunity for jurisdictions that will not meet the compliance
  timelines set forth in SB 1383 to submit a compliance plan to avoid having
  enforcement penalties assessed by the California Department of Resources
  Recycling and Recovery (CalRecycle). The NOIC must be submitted to
  CalRecycle by March 1, 2022, and must include identification of specific
  compliance gaps, actions the City will take to comply, and a timeline for
  implementation. CalRecycle must respond to the NOIC within 45 days, and if
  approved, the City may not be penalized if the tasks detailed in the NOIC are
  completed consistent with the stated timeline. If any deadlines in the compliance
  plan are missed, the City may be fined by Cal Recycle for the amounts accrued for
  non-compliance, beginning January 1, 2022.

  To ensure compliance with SB 1383 and the SLCP Regulations, the City must
  adopt an enforceable ordinance and other mechanisms to ensure that all
  residential and commercial waste generators are compliant with SB 1383
  regulations. Such mechanisms will enable the City to enforce the regulations and
  assess penalties for non-compliance beginning in 2024. Staff will bring forward a
  mandatory recycling and organics ordinance for City Council consideration in
  March 2022. To qualify for State grant funding to assist in implementing SB 1383,
  the City must adopt the ordinance by April 1, 2022.
